title: Growing Jerusalem artichoke
subtitle: A vigorous perennial with high yields and almost no effort after the first planting.
excerpt: Jerusalem artichoke is a tall, vigorous perennial grown for its knobbly tubers. Plant once in spring and harvest from October onwards for several years. It spreads readily: confine it unless you have space for it to expand.
sourceNotes: Growing guidance from RHS (rhs.org.uk) and widely available UK kitchen garden sources. Inulin digestibility note from food science literature. Windbreak value based on plant height data.

glossaryTerms.definition: A type of dietary fibre found in Jerusalem artichoke, chicory, and onions. The human gut cannot digest it directly; gut bacteria ferment it, which can cause bloating and wind, particularly in people who eat it regularly for the first time.

content.text: Jerusalem artichoke is a tall perennial that produces knobbly tubers from October onwards. Plant seed tubers in spring, leave it almost entirely alone through the season, and dig what you need from October to February. It grows 2 to 3 m tall and provides a useful temporary windbreak at the north end of a vegetable plot.

Jerusalem artichoke tolerates almost any soil. It grows in partial shade, though yield is better in full sun. Hardy to H6. The 2 to 3 m height casts shade on anything directly to its south; keep it to the north or west edge of the plot.

Plant seed tubers from February to April, 10 to 15 cm deep, 45 cm apart in rows 90 cm apart. Use small tubers rather than cutting large ones. Water in if the soil is dry. The plants emerge in April or May and grow fast through summer.

Earth up the stems slightly when the plants reach 30 cm tall, as for potatoes. This anchors the tall stems and prevents them rocking in wind. Cut the stems down to 1.5 m in midsummer if they are shading too much of the plot.

Harvest from October once the stems have died back. Dig tubers as needed through autumn and winter rather than lifting them all at once. Tubers left in the ground keep well until March and remain firm. Leave a few tubers in the ground each year for the following season's crop.
Cut and compost the dead stems in late October. The remaining root system decomposes and returns organic matter to the soil over winter.

attrs.title: Containing the spread
attrs.body: Jerusalem artichoke spreads freely if any tuber is left in the ground. This is not a problem in a dedicated bed, but it can crowd out neighbouring plants in a mixed border. To contain it, dig thoroughly at harvest and remove all tubers. A buried root barrier (old slates or corrugated iron laid vertically at the bed edge) stops the roots travelling sideways.
